title: Two Major West Coast Faults May Rupture Together, Study Finds
summary:
Two of the most closely watched fault systems on North America's West Coast may be more connected than scientists previously realized. A recent study suggests that the Cascadia subduction zone and the San Andreas fault can become synchronized, with a major earthquake on one fault potentially followed by seismic activity on the other. In some cases preserved in the geologic record, the two systems may have ruptured only minutes or hours apart.

"We're used to hearing the 'Big One' — Cascadia — being this catastrophic huge thing," said Chris Goldfinger, a marine geologist at Oregon State University and lead author of the study. "It turns out it's not the worst-case scenario."

To investigate, Goldfinger and his colleagues studied deep-sea sediment cores containing about 3,100 years of geologic history. These cylindrical samples preserve layers of material that accumulated on the ocean floor over centuries. Of particular interest were deposits called turbidites, which can form when underwater landslides send large amounts of sediment rushing downhill. Powerful earthquakes are one of the events capable of triggering these submarine landslides.

By comparing turbidite layers associated with the Cascadia and San Andreas fault systems, the researchers found striking similarities in their timing and structure. Those patterns suggest that major earthquakes on the two faults have sometimes occurred unusually close together. Pinning down the exact amount of time between ancient earthquakes is difficult. However, Goldfinger said the team identified three events during the past 1,500 years when Cascadia and the northern San Andreas appear to have ruptured within minutes to hours of each other. The most recent of those episodes occurred around 1700.

The possibility of closely spaced earthquakes could have major consequences for disaster preparation. Even one major rupture along Cascadia or the San Andreas could create an enormous emergency response challenge. If both systems ruptured within a short period, multiple major metropolitan areas could be dealing with severe damage at nearly the same time.

"We could expect that an earthquake on one of the faults alone would draw down the resources of the whole country to respond to it," Goldfinger said. "And if they both went off together, then you've got potentially San Francisco, Portland, Seattle and Vancouver all in an emergency situation in a compressed timeframe."

Scientists have considered for decades whether separate fault systems can synchronize their behavior. Direct observations, however, are extremely rare. Only one example has previously been observed, involving earthquakes in Sumatra that occurred three months apart in 2004 and 2005.

The roots of the new research stretch back to an ocean expedition in 1999. At the time, Goldfinger and his colleagues were collecting sediment cores from the Cascadia subduction zone off Oregon and northern California. A navigational mistake carried their vessel off its intended route, placing the researchers about 55 miles south of Cape Mendocino, California, inside the San Andreas fault region. Rather than abandon the detour, the team decided to drill a sediment core there. That unexpected sample eventually revealed something unusual.
why_it_matters: Millions of people live in cities built on top of these faults, and if two seismic disasters struck close together, the shared national stock of firefighters, engineers and supplies could be overwhelmed — so the study pushes planners to think about worst cases rather than one disaster at a time.

background_read: The Cascadia subduction zone is the offshore boundary where a small ocean plate dives beneath the North American plate, running from northern California past Oregon, Washington and British Columbia. The San Andreas fault is different: it is a mostly horizontal break running through California where two plates slide past each other. Both can produce very large earthquakes, which is why scientists watch them so closely.

Chris Goldfinger, the lead author, is a marine geologist at Oregon State University (a research university in the U.S. Pacific Northwest) — he studies the ocean floor and the layers of mud on top of it instead of digging on land.

The most recent episode the team points to, around 1700, lines up with a well-documented Cascadia earthquake that sent a tsunami across the Pacific Ocean; the wave was recorded in Japan, giving historians an exact date.

Turbidites have been used for decades as a natural archive, because a huge earthquake can shake loose underwater landslides that leave a distinctive sandy layer on the sea floor. Matching those layers across two different faults is one of the few ways to compare earthquakes that happened long before people were writing things down.

Faults triggering each other is rarely observed directly. The only previously documented case involved earthquakes near Sumatra (the Indonesian island where the giant 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake struck), which occurred three months apart in 2004 and 2005.

perspectives.description: If the faults really are linked, emergency planners gain something valuable: a reason to model double disasters and to coordinate response plans across California, Oregon, Washington and British Columbia. Building codes, hospital backup power and evacuation routes could all be tested against a harder scenario.

Turbidite layers are indirect evidence, and dating ancient earthquakes carries large error bars, so 'minutes to hours apart' is an inference rather than something anyone watched happen. Some researchers will want more cores and independent dating methods before treating the two faults as one system.

Seismology has historically studied faults as separate machines, partly because data came from one region at a time. The article itself notes that direct observations of one fault triggering another are extremely rare — only the 2004-2005 Sumatra pair had been documented before. This study is less a discovery of a new hazard than a challenge to the way hazards are traditionally modelled.

The obvious next steps are more offshore drilling, better radiocarbon and tsunami-record dating, and computer models that can simulate two ruptures interacting. If the link holds up, insurance markets, building standards and cross-border emergency agreements may all need updating for a correlated — not independent — risk.
